name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,846

entries.clue: Rank Keith last in project, without further ado (4,4,4)

indicatorNotes.Rank: Rank means rancid, gone off, and letters that have gone off will not stay in the order they were handed over in.
indicatorNotes.in: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the shuffled letters are planted in the middle of the short word that follows.

blocks.note: to project is to jut, as a balcony juts out from a wall
the nine letters of KEITH LAST resettled in another order

annotation.surface: An instruction to put Keith at the bottom of the list for this piece of work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rank Keith last' reads as an order to place him bottom, and rank is the smelly adjective instead. Project is the verb here, and the shuffle breaks its three letters open near the end.
annotation.definitionFit: To do something just like that is to do it on the spot with nothing in between, which is what happens without further ado.

entries.clue: Night-time suits block by modernist architect (7)

blocks.note: a jam is a block — traffic that will not move is jammed
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the last director of the Bauhaus and the man behind the Seagram Building, is known by his middle name alone

annotation.surface: Darkness flattering an apartment block put up by a famous modernist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suits' is a verb in the surface — night-time suits the building — and a plural noun in the answer. Mies van der Rohe is always just Mies once the wordplay has him.
annotation.definitionFit: Jammies is the nursery shortening of pyjamas, the loose two-piece suit worn in bed.

entries.clue: Species of small tortoise seen in odd places to the north (5)

indicatorNotes.seen in odd places: Letters seen in odd places are the first, third, fifth and seventh, so every other letter of the word is stepped over.
indicatorNotes.to the north: North is up the page, so in a down entry everything gathered so far is read from the bottom back up to the top.

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for small, as on a clothing label
the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of TORTOISE

annotation.surface: A small tortoise species recorded at scattered sites further north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Species' is the everyday sense of kinds, not the biological rank the tortoise dangles in front of you. Everything collected is turned round in one go, so the abbreviation ends up at the back.
annotation.definitionFit: Sorts are kinds or varieties — all sorts of people — which is what species means outside the laboratory.

entries.clue: Field sets off with half dropping out (3)

indicatorNotes.half dropping out: Half of something dropping out leaves the other half behind, so a six-letter word arrives with only its first three letters.

blocks.note: a train that sets off leaves, and the last three letters drop away

annotation.surface: A race field starting out with half the entrants withdrawing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Field' is the runners in a race in the surface and grazing land in the answer. Lea is Gray's word in the Elegy — the lowing herd winds slowly o'er the lea.
annotation.definitionFit: A lea is an open stretch of grassland or meadow, a field left to pasture.

entries.clue: Picture card Welshman turned up after king (5)

indicatorNotes.turned up: Turning something up in a down entry means writing it from the bottom towards the top, so the name is read backwards.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after the king is written below him in a down entry, so his letter heads the answer.

blocks.note: k is the letter on the king in both chess and cards
Evan is the Welsh form of John and the standard crossword Welshman

annotation.surface: A Welshman showing up only once the king has arrived.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as arrived and instructs you to write the name the other way round. Knave is the older name for the card now usually called the jack.
annotation.definitionFit: The knave is the court card ranking between the ten and the queen, one of the three picture cards in each suit.

entries.clue: Scrape lady's underwear with Marmite? (5,4)

blocks.note: tights are the close-fitting legwear worn under a skirt
a marmite is a big lidded stewpot, the French word the yeast spread took its name from — there is one drawn on the label

annotation.surface: A jar of Marmite being scraped across a lady's underwear.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the brand name is being read as the ordinary French kitchen word behind it. 'Scrape' is the definition and does none of the scraping the surface pictures.
annotation.definitionFit: A tight spot is a fix with no room to manoeuvre in, which is what a scrape means when you are in one.

entries.clue: American colourist upset East European periodically (2,9)

indicatorNotes.upset: Upset means turned over, and a word turned over in a down entry is written from its last letter up to its first.

blocks.note: a is the dictionary abbreviation for American
someone who tints things is a tinter
the Slavs are the East European peoples — Poles, Czechs, Serbs, Russians

annotation.surface: An American colourist getting an East European annoyed every so often.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Periodically' is the word to watch: it usually tells you to take every second letter, and here it is the definition. 'Upset' reads as annoyed and means write it backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done at intervals happens with gaps between the doings, which is what periodically describes.

entries.clue: E.g. Christie's produce etchings, lithographs, etc in series (8)

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for series, the S of S1 E1
etchings and lithographs are prints, and a printer is what produces them

annotation.surface: An auction house bringing out a sale of prints one after another.
annotation.walkthrough: Christie's the auction house is a front for Linford Christie, the Olympic hundred-metres champion. Etchings and lithographs are both kinds of print, which is what delivers the printer.
annotation.definitionFit: Linford Christie won the 100 metres at the 1992 Olympics, so he is one example of a sprinter — a runner over the short distances.

entries.clue: Eggs sat on by considerate male penguin (6)

indicatorNotes.sat on by: Whatever sits on something is above it, so in a down entry the sitter is written first and what he sits on goes underneath.

blocks.note: a gent is a man, and the courtesy is built into the word
two eggs drawn as two O's

annotation.surface: A thoughtful male penguin taking his turn on the eggs.
annotation.walkthrough: Male penguins really do incubate, so the picture is natural history rather than nonsense. The gentoo is the one with the orange bill and the white flash over the eye.
annotation.definitionFit: The gentoo is one of the brush-tailed penguins of the Antarctic and the sub-Antarctic islands, so penguin names its family.

entries.clue: Nougat confection cooked with sweet wine (7)

blocks.note: a Mars bar is nougat and caramel under chocolate
on a menu a la is the French for done in the style of, as in a la creme

annotation.surface: A nougat dessert simmered in a sweet wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' looks like an anagram instruction and is half of a menu tag instead. Marsala comes from the Sicilian town of that name and is what zabaglione is made with.
annotation.definitionFit: Marsala is the fortified wine of western Sicily, drunk sweet after dinner and used in the kitchen.

entries.clue: Catch sight of naughty kid cutting legs off (7)

indicatorNotes.cutting: To cut into something is to go inside it, so the little devil lands in the middle of the other letters.
indicatorNotes.off: Milk that is off has gone bad, and letters that have gone off will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: the four letters of LEGS resettled, two in front and two behind
an imp is a mischievous child

annotation.surface: A naughty child caught sawing the legs off the furniture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Off' finishes the phrase 'legs off' so neatly that it is easy to miss it doing the shuffling. The imp is crosswords' standard small troublemaker.
annotation.definitionFit: To glimpse something is to catch sight of it for an instant before it is gone again.

entries.clue: Popular figure out with conservationists on the rocks (9)

blocks.note: what is popular is in, as in fashion
to figure something out is to solve it
NT is the National Trust, the charity that owns great stretches of the British coast and countryside

annotation.surface: A celebrity spending the day out among the rocks with conservationists.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Popular figure' reads as one phrase and is torn in two by the wordplay, which takes the verb 'figure out' instead. On the rocks is where a ship ends up as well as a marriage.
annotation.definitionFit: A business on the rocks has run aground and cannot pay, which is what insolvent says of it in the accountant's word.

entries.clue: Act is fool's last during diplomatic mission (11)

indicatorNotes.during: What happens during something happens inside it, so these letters are dropped into the middle of the word named after.

blocks.note: a legation is a diplomatic mission ranking below an embassy
the word is taken as it stands
the last letter of FOOL

annotation.surface: A fool's final turn during a diplomatic visit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Act' is the parliamentary kind, not the performance the fool is putting on. A legation is the smaller sort of embassy, headed by a minister rather than an ambassador.
annotation.definitionFit: Legislation is law as parliament makes it, and a single Act of Parliament is one piece of it.

entries.clue: Wind noodle around middle of chopstick (5)

indicatorNotes.around: What goes around something is wrapped right round it, so the letter named next sits inside.

blocks.note: a noodle is a fool, and so is a twit
chopstick has nine letters, so it has one letter in the middle

annotation.surface: Noodles being wound round the middle of a chopstick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Noodle' is the supper in the surface and an old word for a fool in the wordplay, which is what makes the chopstick look innocent.
annotation.definitionFit: To wind a wire round a post is to twist it, so wind and twist are the same verb.

entries.clue: Doubtfully lift pipe down by carpet (5)

blocks.note: sh is the noise you make when you are telling someone to pipe down
a rug is a small carpet

annotation.surface: Somebody hesitantly lifting a pipe that runs down beside the carpet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pipe down' is plumbing in the surface and a demand for quiet in the wordplay. What gets lifted in the answer is a pair of shoulders.
annotation.definitionFit: To shrug is to raise the shoulders, and the gesture says you neither know nor care — the doubt is part of the word.

entries.clue: Bruce Willis film that's bagged an Oscar released (8)

indicatorNotes.bagged: To bag a thing is to put it in the bag, so what the film bagged is shut up inside the film's title.

blocks.note: Red, the 2010 action comedy with Willis as a retired CIA man
Oscar Wilde — the first name points at the man, the surname supplies the letters

annotation.surface: A Bruce Willis picture that picked up an Academy Award.
annotation.walkthrough: Films bag Oscars all the time, which is exactly what hides the fact that this Oscar is a person. Rewilding is the conservation business of putting land or animals back to the wild.
annotation.definitionFit: An animal that has been rewilded has been let out of captivity and back into the wild, so released covers it.

entries.clue: Water bus manoeuvring at stop-over loses seconds (9)

indicatorNotes.manoeuvring: A boat being manoeuvred is worked this way and that, so these letters will not stay in the order given.
indicatorNotes.loses: What is lost is gone for good, so the letter for the word after it never reaches the answer.

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged
s is the abbreviation for seconds, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A water bus shuffling about at a stopover and running seconds late.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loses seconds' sounds like a timekeeping complaint and is an instruction to drop a letter. A vaporetto is the public boat that works the Venetian canals to a timetable.
annotation.definitionFit: The vaporetti are Venice's public waterbuses, calling at numbered stops along the Grand Canal exactly as a bus does on land.

entries.clue: Fiddle turned into crime (9)

indicatorNotes.turned: Milk that has turned has gone off, and four letters that have turned no longer sit in the order they came in.

blocks.note: a viola is a fiddle, the deeper-voiced member of the violin family
four letters resettled in another order

annotation.surface: A swindle that has grown into something criminal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned into' reads as one phrase and breaks in the middle, with only the last word as fodder. Fiddle is the instrument here, not the swindle the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: A violation is a breach of a law or a right — of a treaty, of parking rules — and a breach of the law is a crime.

entries.clue: Seaside town bluer than any other, frequently (9)

blocks.note: to feel blue is to feel low, so the bluest of the lot is the lowest
oft is the old short form of often

annotation.surface: A resort gloomier than anywhere else on the coast, and gloomy time after time.
annotation.walkthrough: Blue and low are the same word for misery, so the superlative of one is the superlative of the other. Lowestoft is the Suffolk fishing port that is the most easterly town in Britain.
annotation.definitionFit: Lowestoft is a fishing port and holiday resort on the Suffolk coast, sat on the North Sea.

entries.clue: Klutz left masseur without top (6)

indicatorNotes.without top: The top of a word in a down entry is its first letter, and this one has to go without it.

blocks.note: l is the abbreviation for left
a masseur is a rubber, one who rubs you down, and here he loses his r

annotation.surface: A clumsy sort walking out on a topless masseur.
annotation.walkthrough: Rubber for masseur is the old sense of the word, the man at the baths, and it hides behind the bouncy modern one. Landlubber is what keeps lubber alive for the rest of us.
annotation.definitionFit: A lubber is a big clumsy oaf, which is what klutz calls one in American English.

entries.clue: Missile part thinned with file (5)

indicatorNotes.thinned: A plank thinned is shaved down on both faces, so the word before loses a letter from each end.

blocks.note: the two letters left in the middle of PART once both edges have gone
soldiers in single file stand in a row

annotation.surface: Cutting a component down to size with a file.
annotation.walkthrough: The file is the workshop tool in the surface and a line of men in the wordplay, which is what makes the thinning look like carpentry all the way through.
annotation.definitionFit: A missile is anything thrown or shot at a target, and an arrow is what a bow shoots.

entries.clue: How exhilarating to go flat out for stunt (7)

blocks.note: whee is the cry you let out on the way down a helter-skelter
to go flat out is to lie stretched on the ground

annotation.surface: Somebody thrilled at the thought of travelling at top speed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flat out' means at full speed in the surface and stretched on the floor in the wordplay, and the swap is the whole clue. A wheelie is riding along on the back wheel with the front one in the air.
annotation.definitionFit: A wheelie is the trick of lifting a bike's front wheel and riding on the back one, which is a stunt.

entries.clue: Learner in Saab bumped tree (5)

indicatorNotes.bumped: A car that has been bumped has been knocked out of shape, and so have these letters.

blocks.note: the L-plate a British learner driver has to display
four more letters for the shuffle

annotation.surface: A learner driver putting a Saab into a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: The prang is the anagram — 'bumped' does to the letters what it does to the car. Balsa is the featherweight wood that model aeroplanes are built from.
annotation.definitionFit: The balsa is a fast-growing tropical American tree, cut for the lightest timber in commercial use.

entries.clue: Heavens, how quickly a chocolate bar goes (9)

blocks.note: an Aero is the bubbly British chocolate bar, and the answer wants it possessive — a chocolate bar's
the pace of a thing is how quickly it goes

annotation.surface: An exclamation at the speed a bar of chocolate disappears.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is doing the joining: the speed at which an Aero goes is that bar's pace. 'Heavens' is the cry of astonishment and the definition at the same time.
annotation.definitionFit: Aerospace is the earth's atmosphere and the space beyond it taken together, which is the heavens as an engineer divides them up.

entries.clue: Department concerned with charitable donations, mostly (5)

indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly means not quite all of it, so the word in front arrives a letter short.

blocks.note: re means concerning, as at the head of a memo
alms are gifts to the poor, and the s is left off

annotation.surface: A government department that deals with most charitable giving.
annotation.walkthrough: Realm for department is the figurative sense — the realm of physics, not a kingdom. Alms is the old word for money given to the poor and survives in almshouse.
annotation.definitionFit: A realm is a field of activity or knowledge, which is what department means when it is not a place with a front desk.

entries.clue: Bewildered when temperature rises in a constituency (2,3)

indicatorNotes.rises: To rise in a down entry is to climb the page, so the letter for temperature leaves the end of the word it sat in and settles above it.

blocks.note: the clue's own a opens the answer
t is the abbreviation for temperature
a constituency is a seat in Parliament, and SEAT is what is left once the t has gone up

annotation.surface: Confusion in a constituency as the temperature climbs.
annotation.walkthrough: A seat is a constituency in British politics — an MP holds one — and the whole trick is a single letter climbing out of it. Someone all at sea has lost sight of land and of the argument.
annotation.definitionFit: To be at sea is to be out of your depth with nothing to steer by, which is what bewildered describes.

entries.clue: I wear myself out in retirement, like some professors perhaps (7)

indicatorNotes.in retirement: To be in retirement is to have gone back, and letters that have gone back are read from the end to the start.

blocks.note: the speaker of the clue, taken as the letter
to wear myself out is to tire me

annotation.surface: Somebody exhausting themselves even after giving up work.
annotation.walkthrough: Retirement is both what the professors have taken and the instruction to read the wordplay backwards. Emeriti is the Latin plural — one such professor is emeritus.
annotation.definitionFit: Professors who have retired but keep their chair's title are emeriti, so the answer names precisely that group.

entries.clue: In a deep depression, covered with baby's saliva (7)

indicatorNotes.covered with: What is covered lies under what covers it, so the answer is buried in the words that follow.

blocks.note: the run starts on the second letter of the first word and stops three letters into the second, stepping over the apostrophe and the space as if neither were there

annotation.surface: Somebody thoroughly miserable and covered in a baby's dribble.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is stepped over as though it were not there, which is what keeps the buried word out of sight. Abyssal is the zone of the ocean below about four thousand metres.
annotation.definitionFit: The abyssal zone is the deep ocean floor, so abyssal describes whatever lies far down in a trough.

entries.clue: Extras denied lead part, I suppose (3)

indicatorNotes.denied lead part: Denied the leading part means refused the front, so the word loses its first letter.

blocks.note: in cricket a bye is one of the extras, a run scored when the ball beats bat and wicketkeeper alike

annotation.surface: Bit-part actors turned down for the starring role.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extras' are the crowd on a film set in the surface and cricket's extras in the wordplay — the byes, leg byes and wides that are not scored off the bat.
annotation.definitionFit: I suppose is the grudging assent you offer when you mean yes without any enthusiasm for it.

entries.clue: Simple penniless fellow returned, with money in pockets? Certainly (3,2,7)

indicatorNotes.returned: Someone returned has come back the way they went, so the name is written from its last letter round to its first.
indicatorNotes.pockets: To pocket a thing is to slip it inside, so the pieces on either side close over what has just been turned about.

blocks.note: bread with butter is bread and butter
Simple Simon is the nursery-rhyme boy who meets the pieman with not a penny on him
the take is the money taken in at the door

annotation.surface: A broke simpleton coming home with his pockets full of cash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penniless' identifies the boy rather than removing anything — Simon tells the pieman he has not any. The two outer pieces shut over him from both sides at once.
annotation.definitionFit: And no mistake is the tag added to insist on what you have just said — it was cold, and no mistake — so it means certainly.
